intro: In the twentieth century, two kinds of movements promised to remake whole societies. On the far left, communists promised equality and an end to exploitation. On the far right, fascists and Nazis promised national glory, order and unity under one leader. Millions of people believed these promises. Tens of millions died under the governments they built.

This unit looks at both extremes with the same care. You will meet a farmer in Ukraine, a teacher in Berlin, students in Beijing and fighters in the Warsaw Ghetto. You will see why people were drawn to these movements, what the regimes did in power, and how people resisted them. You will also meet Hannah Arendt, who argued that the far left and far right shared a new kind of rule.

By the end you will be able to explain the key ideas of communism and fascism, describe their real record with facts and numbers, and compare them fairly. You will also be able to use evidence to argue about why democracies fail and what protects people's rights.
bigQuestion: How did movements that promised a perfect society end in dictatorship and mass murder, and what can protect people from them?

title: The Extremes: Communism and Fascism

chapters.title: Communism in Power
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did a movement that promised equality and an end to exploitation produce some of the deadliest governments of the twentieth century?

story.title: The Last of the Grain
story.kicker: In the fall of 1932 a farmer in Soviet Ukraine watches officials search his house for food.
paragraphs: Picture a village in central Ukraine in November 1932. A farmer we will call Mykola stands in his yard with his wife and two children. A few years earlier the family worked its own fields. Now the land belongs to the collective farm. Mykola works there with his neighbors, and the state decides how much grain the farm must hand over.

The quota this year is far too high. The harvest was poor, and the farm cannot meet it. So a brigade of officials and local activists goes from house to house. They carry long metal rods. They push the rods into the dirt floors and the walls, feeling for hidden sacks. They take the grain Mykola saved for winter. Then they take the beans and the dried peas.

Mykola is not a rich man. He owns one cow and a small garden. But the officials call anyone who hides food a saboteur, an enemy of the people. A new law allows long prison terms, or even death, for taking grain from collective fields. People call it the law of five ears of wheat, because gleaning a handful could bring a heavy sentence.

That winter and spring, hunger spread across Ukraine. Villages that failed their quotas were put on blacklists and cut off from goods. In January 1933 the government also stopped most peasants from leaving Ukraine to look for food. Millions of people died. Ukrainians today call this the Holodomor, which means death by hunger.

Mykola lived under a government that said it spoke for workers and peasants. Its leaders believed they were building a fair society with no rich and no poor. This chapter asks how that dream turned into the scene in Mykola's yard.
story.think: The officials in the story believed, or said they believed, that they were serving a just cause. What makes it possible for ordinary people to carry out orders that cause great harm?

sections.title: From an Idea to a Revolution

lessons.title: Marx's Promise
lessons.mainIdea: Karl Marx argued that history is a struggle between classes and that workers would one day overthrow owners and share all property.
reading: In the 1840s Karl Marx, a German writer, lived in cities full of new factories. He saw children working long shifts and families crowded into one room. Factory owners grew rich, while workers earned barely enough to eat. Marx asked why a world that made so much wealth left so many people poor.

His answer was *class struggle*. Marx said every society splits into groups based on who owns the means of production, such as land, mines and factories. In his day, owners formed the bourgeoisie. The workers who sold their labor formed the *proletariat*. Marx believed owners kept part of the value workers made, and he called this exploitation.

Marx predicted that workers would rise up, take the factories and share them. In time, he wrote, a *communist* society would have no classes, no private ownership of factories and, in the end, no need for a state at all. Supporters saw a vision of justice. Critics said it ignored human nature and gave no plan for protecting freedom along the way.

words.d: Marx's idea that history is driven by conflict between groups that own property and groups that work for them
in Marx's writing, the working class who sell their labor for wages
describing a society, or a movement toward one, where property is shared in common and classes disappear

look.title: The Opening Claim of the Manifesto
look.text: The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
look.cite: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848), English translation by Samuel Moore, 1888
look.prompt: Put this sentence in your own words. What does Marx think is the main force that shapes history?

check.q: What did Marx call the working class who sell their labor for wages?
check.why: In Marx's writing the proletariat are wage workers; the bourgeoisie are the owners.

check.q: According to the reading, what problem was Marx trying to explain?
choices: Why kings lost power to elected parliaments
Why factories made great wealth while many workers stayed poor
Why farming spread from the Middle East to Europe
Why Germany had many small states
check.why: The reading says Marx asked why a world that made so much wealth left so many people poor.

check.q: What was one criticism of Marx's vision named in the reading?
choices: It praised factory owners too much
It said classes could never disappear
It gave no plan for protecting freedom along the way
It was written only for farmers
check.why: Critics said Marx ignored human nature and gave no plan for protecting freedom during the change.

lessons.title: Lenin and the Revolution of 1917
lessons.mainIdea: In 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Russia and began building a state run by one party in the name of the workers.
reading: In early 1917 Russia was losing badly in World War I. Bread lines stretched through the capital, Petrograd. Workers and soldiers rebelled, and Tsar Nicholas II gave up his throne in March. A temporary government took over, but it kept fighting the war and could not end the hunger.

Vladimir Lenin led a small, disciplined party called the Bolsheviks. Lenin added a key idea to Marx. He said workers would not rise up on their own. They needed a *vanguard party* of full-time revolutionaries to lead them. This blend of ideas became known as *Marxism-Leninism*. In November 1917 the Bolsheviks seized power with the slogan Peace, Land and Bread.

Lenin's government soon shut down rival parties and newspapers. It closed an elected assembly in January 1918 after the Bolsheviks failed to win a majority in it. A secret police called the Cheka arrested and shot opponents. A brutal civil war followed until about 1921. In 1922 the new state was named the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, or USSR. Supporters saw a workers' victory. Critics saw a new dictatorship.

words.d: Lenin's idea of a small group of dedicated revolutionaries who lead the working class
Marx's ideas combined with Lenin's plan for rule by a single revolutionary party
Lenin's party, which took power in Russia in November 1917 and later became the Communist Party

look.title: Two Views of November 1917
look.text: A Bolshevik factory worker says: For the first time, people like me run the country. The war will end and the land will go to those who farm it. A Russian voter says: I voted in the assembly election. When the Bolsheviks lost, they closed the assembly with soldiers. Who decides for the workers now?
look.prompt: What does each speaker value most? Using the reading, explain which facts support each view.

check.q: What was Lenin's idea of a vanguard party?
choices: An army that guards the border
A party that shares power with the tsar
A small group of dedicated revolutionaries who lead the workers
check.why: Lenin said workers needed a vanguard party of full-time revolutionaries to lead them.

check.q: What slogan did the Bolsheviks use in 1917?
check.why: The Bolsheviks promised Peace, Land and Bread to war-weary, hungry Russians.

check.q: What did Lenin's government do after it failed to win a majority in the elected assembly?
choices: It handed power to the winners
check.why: The reading says the Bolsheviks closed the elected assembly in January 1918.

lessons.title: One Party and Collective Farms
lessons.mainIdea: Under Stalin, one party controlled all of Soviet life and forced peasants onto collective farms at a terrible cost.
reading: After Lenin died in 1924, Joseph Stalin outmaneuvered his rivals. By about 1929 he held nearly total power. The Communist Party was the only legal party. It ran the government, the army, the newspapers, the schools and the unions. A system in which one party rules and no rival is allowed is called a *one-party state*.

Stalin wanted to turn a farming country into an industrial power fast. His Five-Year Plans built steel mills, dams and whole new cities. To feed the workers and sell grain abroad, he forced peasants to give up their own plots and join *collective farms*. The state set what they grew and how much they handed over.

Many peasants resisted. Some slaughtered their animals rather than give them up. Stalin blamed better-off farmers, called kulaks, and ordered them removed as a class. Well over a million people were deported to remote regions. Soviet factories grew quickly, and supporters pointed to that growth. Critics point to the hunger, the lost freedom and the lives it cost.

words.d: a country where only one political party is allowed to exist and rule
large farms owned or controlled by the state, where peasants worked together and handed over set amounts of their harvest
the Soviet label for better-off peasants, used to target them for arrest and deportation

look.title: A Five-Year Plan Poster in Words
look.text: Picture a bright Soviet poster from about 1930. A smiling worker stands in front of smoking factory chimneys and a new tractor. Big red letters promise to finish the Five-Year Plan in four years. There are no hungry villages in the picture.
look.prompt: What does this poster want viewers to feel? What does it leave out, based on the reading?

check.q: What is a one-party state?
choices: A country with two parties that take turns
A country where only one party is allowed to exist and rule
A country ruled by a king and a parliament
check.why: A one-party state allows no rival parties; in the USSR only the Communist Party was legal.

check.q: Why did Stalin force peasants onto collective farms?
choices: To give each peasant family more land of its own
To return land to the old nobles
To control grain to feed workers and sell abroad for rapid industry
check.why: The reading says collectivization aimed to feed workers and earn money for fast industrial growth.

check.q: Who were the kulaks in Soviet language?
choices: Better-off peasants targeted for arrest and deportation
check.why: Kulak was the label for better-off peasants, whom Stalin ordered removed as a class.

lessons.title: The Holodomor
lessons.mainIdea: In 1932 and 1933 Soviet grain policies caused a famine in Ukraine that killed millions of people.
reading: Collectivization disrupted farming across the USSR, and hunger struck several regions, including Kazakhstan. In Ukraine the famine of 1932 and 1933 was especially deadly. Grain quotas stayed high even as people starved. Brigades searched homes and took seed grain and other food, as in the chapter's opening story.

Several policies made things worse. Villages that missed quotas were blacklisted and cut off from stores. In January 1933 most peasants were barred from leaving Ukraine to find food. Meanwhile the USSR kept exporting grain. Scholars estimate that roughly 3.5 to 5 million people died in Ukraine. Ukrainians call the famine the *Holodomor*, death by hunger.

Historians still debate one question. Was the famine a deliberate *genocide* aimed at Ukrainians as a nation, or a crime of brutal policy aimed at peasants everywhere? Ukraine and many other countries, including the United States, have officially called it a genocide. Some historians stress Stalin's fear of Ukrainian nationalism. Others stress the wider war on the peasantry. All agree the deaths were caused by human decisions.

words.d: the famine in Soviet Ukraine in 1932 and 1933, whose name means death by hunger
acts carried out to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group
a fixed amount that must be produced or handed over

look.title: Two Historians Disagree
look.text: Historian A: The rules that trapped peasants inside Ukraine and the blacklists on villages show the famine targeted Ukrainians as a people. Historian B: Peasants also starved in Kazakhstan and southern Russia. Stalin's war was against the peasantry as a class, and Ukraine suffered most because it grew the most grain.
look.prompt: Which facts from the reading does each historian use? What further evidence would help you judge between them?

check.q: What does the word Holodomor mean?
check.why: Holodomor is the Ukrainian name for the 1932 to 1933 famine and means death by hunger.

check.q: Which policy in the reading kept starving Ukrainian peasants from finding food elsewhere?
choices: A rule that all grain be sold to Poland
A law giving each family a new cow
A ban on most peasants leaving Ukraine in January 1933
A plan to move factories into Ukraine
check.why: The reading says most peasants were barred from leaving Ukraine to look for food.

check.q: What question about the Holodomor do historians still debate?
choices: Whether any people died at all
Whether it happened in the 1800s or the 1900s
Whether it was caused by a volcano
Whether it was a genocide aimed at Ukrainians as a nation or a wider war on peasants
check.why: The debate is over intent; all agree human decisions caused the deaths.

lessons.title: The Gulag and the Great Terror
lessons.mainIdea: Stalin's regime sent millions to labor camps and, in 1937 and 1938, executed hundreds of thousands of people it called enemies.
reading: The *Gulag* was the Soviet system of forced labor camps. Prisoners cut timber, dug canals and mined gold in freezing places such as Kolyma in the far northeast. Many had done nothing a free country would call a crime. A joke about Stalin, a late arrival at work or a relative abroad could be enough.

In 1937 and 1938 the arrests became a flood called the *Great Terror*. The secret police, then called the NKVD, worked from quotas of enemies to find in each region. Old Bolsheviks confessed to wild charges at public *show trials*. Army officers, engineers, poets and ordinary workers were arrested. Soviet records later showed that roughly 680,000 people were shot in those two years.

Writers who survived told the world. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, a former prisoner, described camp life in One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, published in 1962. Later he wrote The Gulag Archipelago. After the USSR opened its archives around 1991, historians confirmed much of what survivors had said.

words.d: the Soviet system of forced labor camps, from a Russian abbreviation for the camp administration
Stalin's wave of mass arrests and executions in 1937 and 1938
public trials where the verdict is decided in advance and the accused are pressured to confess

look.title: The Scale of Stalin's Repression (rounded)
rows: People who passed through the Gulag, 1930-53
look.cite: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History, 2003; Soviet archival figures cited by historians
look.prompt: Which number is largest? Why might a camp system that held many people at once still be smaller than the total who passed through it?

check.q: What was the Gulag?
choices: The Soviet system of forced labor camps
check.why: The Gulag was the network of forced labor camps, such as those at Kolyma.

check.q: What happened at a show trial?
choices: A jury of workers freely weighed the evidence
The verdict was decided in advance and the accused were pushed to confess
check.why: Show trials were staged for the public with the outcome fixed beforehand.

check.q: How did historians confirm survivors' accounts of the camps?
choices: They relied only on Stalin's speeches
They studied Soviet archives opened around 1991
They counted votes from Soviet elections
check.why: The reading says the archives opened around 1991 confirmed much of what survivors reported.

lessons.title: Mao and the Great Leap Forward
lessons.mainIdea: Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward tried to transform China overnight and caused the deadliest famine in recorded history.
reading: Mao Zedong's Communist Party won China's civil war in 1949. Many peasants welcomed land reform, which took land from landlords and gave it to poor farmers. The reform was also violent. Large numbers of landlords were killed at village meetings. Within a few years, the land was pooled again into collectives.

In 1958 Mao launched the *Great Leap Forward*. He wanted China to pass Britain in steel output within about fifteen years. Villages were merged into huge *people's communes*. Families ate in shared canteens. Millions of peasants left the fields to melt pots and tools in small backyard furnaces. Much of the iron they made was useless.

Local officials, afraid of punishment, reported record harvests that did not exist. The state took grain based on those false numbers. From 1959 to 1961, famine swept the countryside. Scholars' estimates of the deaths range from about 15 million to 45 million, and many cite around 30 million. When the defense minister, Peng Dehuai, raised concerns in 1959, Mao purged him.

words.d: Mao's 1958 to 1962 campaign to speed up farming and industry in China, which caused a massive famine
very large rural units in Mao's China that combined many villages and controlled work, food and daily life
taking land from large owners and giving it to farmers who work it

look.title: Estimates of Deaths in the Great Leap Famine
look.cite: Banister, China's Changing Population, 1987; Yang, Tombstone, 2008; Dikotter, Mao's Great Famine, 2010
look.prompt: Why might careful scholars reach different totals? What do all three estimates agree on?

check.q: What was a people's commune?
choices: A city council elected by voters
A factory owned by a foreign company
A huge rural unit that joined many villages and controlled work and food
check.why: Communes merged villages and ran daily life, including shared canteens.

check.q: Why did the state take too much grain during the Great Leap?
choices: Officials reported false record harvests out of fear
Peasants voted to give away their grain
A war with Britain cut off food
China had no farms at the time
check.why: The reading says frightened officials inflated harvests, and grain was taken based on those numbers.

check.q: What happened to Peng Dehuai when he raised concerns in 1959?
choices: He was made head of the communes
He was sent to study in Moscow as a reward
check.why: Mao removed the defense minister for criticizing the campaign.

lessons.title: The Cultural Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: From 1966 Mao urged young Red Guards to attack teachers, officials and old traditions, throwing China into a decade of turmoil.
reading: Picture a middle school in Beijing in 1966. Students paste large handwritten posters on the walls accusing their teachers of being enemies of the revolution. Some teachers are forced to wear dunce caps and are beaten. A few are killed. This was the start of the *Cultural Revolution*, which lasted until Mao's death in 1976.

Mao, sidelined after the Great Leap, wanted to regain control and keep the revolution alive. He called on young *Red Guards* to smash the Four Olds: old customs, culture, habits and ideas. They wrecked temples, burned books and paraded officials in public *struggle sessions*, where a person was shouted at, humiliated and forced to confess.

A *cult of personality* surrounded Mao. Millions carried his Little Red Book of quotations. Schools and universities closed for years. Millions of city youths were later sent to the countryside to learn from peasants. Deaths are estimated in the hundreds of thousands at least, and some scholars estimate far more. China's later leaders officially called the period a grave mistake.

words.d: Mao's 1966 to 1976 campaign to purge rivals and old ways of thinking, which caused widespread violence
young people who answered Mao's call to attack enemies of the revolution
public meetings where a person was humiliated and forced to confess to political crimes
the use of propaganda to present a leader as heroic, wise and beyond criticism

look.title: A Student's Choice
look.text: You are fifteen in 1966. Your class is writing a poster that accuses your math teacher of being a class enemy. She once gave you extra help after school. Everyone is watching to see whether you sign. Refusing could mark you as an enemy too.
look.prompt: What pressures does this student face? How does this scene help explain why ordinary people took part in the Cultural Revolution?

check.q: What were the Four Olds that Red Guards attacked?
choices: Old farms, factories, mines and railroads
Old kings, priests, soldiers and judges
Old customs, culture, habits and ideas
Old books, songs, maps and coins only
check.why: Mao told Red Guards to smash old customs, culture, habits and ideas.

check.q: What is a cult of personality?
choices: A religious group that rejects all leaders
A vote to remove a leader
Propaganda that presents a leader as heroic and beyond criticism
check.why: The Little Red Book and endless praise of Mao are examples of a cult of personality.

check.q: How did China's later leaders officially describe the Cultural Revolution?
check.why: The reading says China's later leaders officially called it a grave mistake.

lessons.title: The Khmer Rouge in Cambodia
lessons.mainIdea: From 1975 to 1979 the Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia's cities and killed or starved about 1.5 to 2 million people.
reading: On April 17, 1975, Khmer Rouge soldiers entered Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia. Within days they ordered the whole city, well over a million people, to march into the countryside. The sick were pushed out of hospitals. The new rulers, led by Pol Pot, declared Year Zero, a complete break with the past.

The Khmer Rouge wanted a pure society of peasants with no money, markets, schools or religion. People worked on farms from dawn to night under guard. Teachers, doctors, monks, people who wore glasses and ethnic minorities such as Vietnamese and Cham Muslims were targeted. Mass graves later found across the country became known as the *killing fields*.

At a former school in Phnom Penh called S-21, or Tuol Sleng, thousands of prisoners were photographed, tortured and killed. Scholars estimate that about 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians died from execution, starvation, overwork and disease. That was roughly a fifth of the population. The regime fell when Vietnam invaded in January 1979. It is widely described as an *autogenocide*, a people destroyed by rulers from its own nation.

words.d: the Communist movement led by Pol Pot that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979
the mass grave sites across Cambodia where the Khmer Rouge buried its victims
a term for mass killing carried out by a government against large parts of its own people

look.title: Cambodia Under the Khmer Rouge (rounded)
look.unit: million people; years in power in years
look.cite: Ben Kiernan, The Pol Pot Regime, 1996; Yale University Cambodian Genocide Program
look.prompt: About what share of the population died? Show how you worked it out.

check.q: What did the Khmer Rouge do right after taking Phnom Penh?
choices: Forced the whole city to march into the countryside
check.why: The reading says the whole city was ordered into the countryside within days.

check.q: Which groups did the Khmer Rouge target, according to the reading?
choices: Only members of the Khmer Rouge
Teachers, doctors, monks and ethnic minorities
Only people who lived in Vietnam
check.why: Educated people, monks and minorities like the Cham were singled out.

check.q: How did Khmer Rouge rule end?
choices: The United Nations bought the country
Cambodian peasants voted it out in 1975
check.why: The regime fell when Vietnamese forces invaded in January 1979.

lessons.title: Cuba and North Korea
lessons.mainIdea: Communist governments still rule in Cuba and North Korea, each with its own history of promises and repression.
reading: In 1959 Fidel Castro's rebels overthrew Cuba's dictator, Fulgencio Batista. Castro soon declared the revolution socialist and allied with the USSR. His government expanded schooling and free health care, and it ran a large literacy campaign in 1961. Supporters still point to these gains.

Castro's Cuba also became a one-party state. Independent newspapers were closed, and critics were jailed. Private businesses were taken over. Well over a million Cubans have left the island since 1959, many for Florida. Critics describe a country where people lack free speech and free elections.

North Korea was founded in 1948 under Kim Il Sung. His son and grandson have ruled since. The state teaches *Juche*, or self-reliance, and surrounds the Kim family with a cult of personality. A famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands of people, by many estimates. A United Nations inquiry in 2014 reported vast political prison camps. North Korea is often called the most closed country on earth.

words.d: North Korea's official idea of national self-reliance
an organized effort to teach large numbers of people to read and write
a ruler with total power who is not limited by elections or courts

look.title: A United Nations Finding
look.text: The inquiry found that North Korea commits systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations, including a network of political prison camps, on a scale without parallel in the modern world.
look.cite: United Nations Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Report, 2014 (summary)
look.prompt: What kind of evidence would a commission need to reach this finding about a closed country? Why might that be hard to gather?

check.q: Whom did Fidel Castro's rebels overthrow in 1959?
check.why: Castro's rebels overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista.

check.q: What does Juche mean in North Korea?
check.why: Juche is North Korea's official idea of national self-reliance.

check.q: Which gain do supporters of Cuba's government point to?
choices: Expanded schooling and free health care
check.why: The reading names schooling, free health care and the 1961 literacy campaign.

lessons.title: Why People Were Drawn to It
lessons.mainIdea: Communism attracted people with real hopes for equality, land and dignity, even as its record in power turned out very differently.
reading: Imagine a landless farmworker in China in the 1940s. He pays half his crop to a landlord and owes money he can never repay. A Communist organizer arrives and promises land of his own. For people like him, the offer was powerful. Communism spoke to real suffering.

Across the world, communism promised *equality*, an end to *exploitation*, jobs for all and freedom from foreign rule. In colonies, it offered a way to fight empires. In the 1930s, when capitalist countries sank into the Great Depression, the USSR claimed to have no unemployment. Some Western writers visited and praised it, often without seeing the famines.

In power, the pattern was often the same. A single party claimed to know the one true path. Anyone who disagreed became an enemy. With no free press, courts or elections to check them, leaders made disastrous choices and no one could stop them. Defenders of socialist ideas argue that these regimes betrayed Marx's goals. Critics argue that concentrating all economic and political power made abuse likely.

words.d: the state of people having the same rights, status or share
unfairly using someone's work for another person's gain
limits, such as courts, elections and a free press, that stop leaders from abusing power

look.title: Promise and Record
look.text: Promise: land for peasants. Record: land taken back into collectives and communes. Promise: power to the workers. Record: power held by one party and its leader. Promise: an end to hunger. Record: the Holodomor and the Great Leap famine.
look.prompt: Pick one pair. Using facts from the chapter, explain why the promise and the record came apart.

check.q: Why did communism appeal to many landless farmworkers?
choices: It promised to keep landlords in charge
It promised to end all farming
It promised them land of their own
check.why: The reading's example is a farmworker drawn by the promise of his own land.

check.q: Why did the USSR look attractive to some people in the 1930s?
choices: It claimed to have no unemployment during the Great Depression
It held free elections every year
It had the world's largest navy
check.why: When capitalist countries faced mass unemployment, the USSR claimed full employment.

check.q: What argument do critics make about why these regimes turned abusive?
choices: They had too many political parties
Concentrating all economic and political power made abuse likely
Their newspapers criticized leaders too much
check.why: Critics say that with no checks on concentrated power, abuse became likely.

lessons.title: The Wall Falls
lessons.mainIdea: In 1989 the Berlin Wall fell and Eastern European communist governments collapsed; in 1991 the Soviet Union itself broke apart.
reading: On the night of November 9, 1989, East German officials announced, by mistake, that their citizens could cross the border freely. Crowds rushed to the *Berlin Wall*, which had divided the city since 1961. Guards opened the gates. People climbed on the wall and chipped pieces off with hammers.

The fall came after years of pressure. Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader from 1985, allowed more open talk, called *glasnost*, and tried economic reform. In Poland the Solidarity trade union, led by Lech Walesa, won partly free elections in 1989. That year communist rule ended across Eastern Europe, mostly without bloodshed. Romania was the violent exception.

In 1991 the USSR broke into fifteen independent countries, including Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan. The Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin on December 25. China's Communist Party kept power, but it crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in June 1989 and later opened its economy to markets. The Cold War contest between communism and the West was over.

words.d: the guarded wall that divided East and West Berlin from 1961 to 1989
Gorbachev's policy of greater openness and freer discussion in the USSR
the independent Polish trade union that led peaceful opposition to communist rule

look.title: Two Crowds in 1989
look.text: In November, a crowd in Berlin climbs the wall while guards stand aside. In June, a crowd of students in Beijing's Tiananmen Square is cleared by tanks and soldiers. Both crowds wanted more freedom.
look.prompt: Why might the two events have ended so differently? Use at least one fact from the reading.

check.q: What was glasnost?
check.why: Glasnost was Gorbachev's policy of freer discussion.

check.q: Which Eastern European country's change in 1989 was violent, according to the reading?
check.why: The reading calls Romania the violent exception.

check.q: What happened to the USSR in 1991?
choices: It broke into fifteen independent countries
check.why: The USSR dissolved into fifteen countries, and its flag came down on December 25, 1991.

review.q: Which idea did Lenin add to Marx's theory?
choices: A vanguard party of revolutionaries must lead the workers
review.why: Lenin's vanguard party idea is the core of Marxism-Leninism.

choices: The 1932 to 1933 famine in Soviet Ukraine
review.why: The Holodomor was the famine in Ukraine caused by Soviet grain policies.

choices: Great Leap Forward and Mao Zedong
review.why: Mao launched the Great Leap; the Terror was Stalin's, Year Zero Pol Pot's and Juche North Korea's.

choices: Life in the Soviet labor camps
The fall of the Berlin Wall
review.why: Solzhenitsyn, a former prisoner, wrote about the Gulag.

review.q: How did the Khmer Rouge regime differ from Castro's Cuba?
choices: It abolished money and schools and killed about a fifth of the population
It expanded schooling and health care
It allied with the United States
review.why: The Khmer Rouge abolished money, schools and religion; Cuba expanded schooling while limiting freedom.

review.q: What common pattern does the chapter find in communist states in power?
choices: One party claimed the true path and removed all checks on its power
review.why: With no press, courts or elections to check them, leaders' disastrous choices went unstopped.

review.q: Which fact about the Great Leap famine do all scholars in the chapter agree on?
choices: Tens of millions of people died
review.why: Estimates range from about 15 to 45 million, but all show a catastrophic toll.

review.q: What happened on the night of November 9, 1989?
choices: Crowds crossed the Berlin Wall after the border was opened
Khmer Rouge soldiers entered Phnom Penh
review.why: An announcement opened the border, and crowds crossed the Berlin Wall.

chapters.title: Fascism and Nazism
chapters.bigQuestion: How did movements that glorified the nation and the leader destroy democracy and carry out mass murder, and why did so many people follow them?

story.title: The List on the Library Door
story.kicker: In the spring of 1933 a Berlin teacher is handed a list of books that must leave the school.
paragraphs: Imagine a high school in Berlin in April 1933. A literature teacher we will call Fraulein Weber arrives early and finds a typed list pinned to the library door. The heading says the books below are un-German. They must be removed at once. Hitler has been chancellor for less than three months.

She reads the names. Heinrich Heine, a poet her students memorize. Erich Maria Remarque, whose novel All Quiet on the Western Front tells the truth about the trenches. Erich Kastner, who writes funny, kind books for children. Some are Jewish. Some are pacifists. Some are simply writers the new government dislikes.

In the hallway a colleague tells her quietly that the Jewish science teacher has been dismissed. A new law removes Jews and political opponents from government jobs, and public schools count. Several students now wear the uniform of the Hitler Youth. One of them offers to help carry the books out.

On the night of May 10, 1933, student groups across Germany burn tens of thousands of books in public squares. In Berlin a crowd watches a bonfire in front of the university. Fraulein Weber has a choice. She can hide a few books at home. She can say nothing. She can speak up and likely lose her job.

A century earlier, Heine had written in a play that where people burn books, they will in the end burn people too. This chapter follows how that warning came true, and asks how a modern, educated country let it happen.
story.think: What small choices did the teacher and her students face? How can many small choices add up to something very large?

lessons.title: The March on Rome
lessons.mainIdea: Benito Mussolini used street violence and the fear of revolution to take power in Italy in 1922 and build the first fascist state.
reading: After World War I, many Italians felt cheated. Italy had been on the winning side, yet the peace treaties gave it less land than it had hoped. Prices rose, and workers held strikes and took over factories in 1919 and 1920. Property owners feared a revolution like Russia's.

Benito Mussolini, a former socialist newspaper editor, founded the *fascist* movement in 1919. The name came from the fasces, a bundle of rods carried in ancient Rome as a sign of authority. His armed squads, called Blackshirts, beat up socialists and burned union halls. Many police and landowners looked the other way or helped.

In October 1922 thousands of Blackshirts gathered for a March on Rome. King Victor Emmanuel III refused to use the army against them and asked Mussolini to become prime minister. By 1926 Italy was a *one-party state*. Other parties were banned, and newspapers were controlled. Mussolini took the title Il Duce, the leader.

words.d: describing a movement that puts the nation above the individual, rules through one party and one leader, and uses violence against opponents
Mussolini's armed squads, who used violence against socialists and other opponents
a country where only one political party is allowed to exist and rule

look.title: A Landowner's View in 1921
look.text: A landowner near Bologna says: The socialists took over the town council and the workers struck at harvest. The police did nothing. Then the Blackshirts came, and the strikes stopped. I do not like their clubs and their shouting, but they brought order.
look.prompt: What does this speaker want most? What is he willing to overlook to get it, and what might that cost him later?

check.q: Where does the word fascist come from?
choices: The fasces, a bundle of rods that stood for authority in ancient Rome
check.why: The fasces was an ancient Roman symbol of authority that Mussolini borrowed.

check.q: Why did many property owners support Mussolini's squads?
choices: They wanted Italy to join the USSR
They feared a socialist revolution after strikes and factory takeovers
They hoped to give land to peasants
check.why: Strikes and factory occupations in 1919 and 1920 made owners fear a revolution like Russia's.

check.q: What did King Victor Emmanuel III do during the March on Rome?
choices: He led the army against the Blackshirts
He refused to use the army and asked Mussolini to be prime minister
check.why: The king declined to stop the march and appointed Mussolini.

lessons.title: The Leader and the Total State
lessons.mainIdea: Italian Fascism built a cult around Mussolini, demanded that all of life serve the state, and used violence to silence critics.
reading: In 1924 Giacomo Matteotti, a socialist member of parliament, stood up and accused the Fascists of cheating in that year's election. Days later, Fascist thugs kidnapped and murdered him. Mussolini at first seemed in trouble. Then in January 1925 he told parliament that he took responsibility for what had happened, and he moved to crush all opposition.

Mussolini described his goal as a total state, where every part of life served the nation. Schools taught children to believe, obey and fight. Youth groups trained boys for war. Posters showed Il Duce as an athlete, farmer and soldier. This *cult of the leader* told people that one man embodied the whole nation.

Supporters praised Fascism for order, national pride and new public works. The claim that Mussolini made the trains run on time was popular, though historians doubt it. Critics saw jailed opponents, a controlled press and, from 1935, a brutal war of conquest in Ethiopia. In 1938 Italy passed anti-Jewish racial laws, and it joined Hitler's war in 1940.

words.d: propaganda that presents one leader as the heroic embodiment of the nation
Mussolini's idea of a state that controls or directs every part of life
information, often one-sided or false, spread to shape what people think

look.title: Mussolini's Formula
look.text: Everything within the state, nothing outside the state, nothing against the state.
look.cite: Benito Mussolini, speech to the Chamber of Deputies, 1927, as commonly translated
look.prompt: What room does this formula leave for a free press, an independent church or an opposition party? Explain.

check.q: Who was Giacomo Matteotti?
choices: A socialist member of parliament murdered after accusing the Fascists of election fraud
check.why: Matteotti denounced Fascist cheating in 1924 and was killed by Fascist thugs.

check.q: What does cult of the leader mean?
choices: A religious group that rejects politics
Propaganda that presents one leader as the heroic embodiment of the nation
A group of leaders who share power equally
A vote to choose a new leader
check.why: Posters of Mussolini as athlete, farmer and soldier are examples.

check.q: Which fact from the reading do critics of Fascist Italy point to?
choices: A brutal war of conquest in Ethiopia from 1935
check.why: Critics point to the Ethiopian war, jailed opponents and a controlled press.

lessons.title: Why Germans Turned to Hitler
lessons.mainIdea: National humiliation, economic disaster and fear of communism helped Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party grow from a fringe group to Germany's largest party.
reading: Picture a Berlin family in 1923. Prices double every few days. A loaf of bread that cost a few marks costs billions by November. Their savings are worthless. This *hyperinflation* followed Germany's defeat in World War I and the Treaty of Versailles, which took land and demanded large payments called reparations.

Many Germans believed a false story that the army had been stabbed in the back by traitors at home, especially Jews and socialists. Adolf Hitler, leader of the National Socialist German Workers' Party, or Nazis, spread that myth. After a failed coup in Munich in 1923, he chose to win power through elections.

Then the *Great Depression* hit in 1929. By 1932 about six million Germans were out of work. Communist and Nazi fighters clashed in the streets. Many middle-class voters, farmers and business leaders feared a communist revolution. The Nazi vote soared. In January 1933, conservative politicians persuaded President Hindenburg to make Hitler chancellor, hoping they could control him.

words.d: extremely fast price rises that make money almost worthless
payments a defeated country is made to pay for war damage
the worldwide economic collapse that began in 1929 and caused mass unemployment
the head of the German government

look.title: Nazi Share of the Vote in Reichstag Elections
look.cite: Official German Reichstag election results, as reported by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum and standard histories
look.prompt: When did the Nazi vote rise fastest? Link that jump to an event in the reading. Did the Nazis ever win a majority in these elections?

check.q: What is hyperinflation?
choices: A sudden drop in the number of workers
Extremely fast price rises that make money almost worthless
check.why: In 1923 German prices rose so fast that savings became worthless.

check.q: About how many Germans were out of work by 1932?
check.why: The reading says about six million Germans were unemployed by 1932.

check.q: Why did conservative politicians help make Hitler chancellor?
choices: He had won a clear majority of all votes
They hoped they could control him
check.why: Conservatives believed they could use and contain Hitler; they were wrong.

lessons.title: Destroying a Democracy
lessons.mainIdea: Within months in 1933, the Nazis used emergency powers, terror and new laws to turn a democracy into a dictatorship.
reading: On February 27, 1933, the Reichstag, Germany's parliament building, caught fire. Hitler blamed the communists. The next day an emergency decree suspended freedom of speech, the press and assembly. Police arrested thousands of communists and socialists. The first *concentration camp* opened at Dachau in March 1933.

On March 23, 1933, the Reichstag passed the *Enabling Act*. It let Hitler's government make laws without parliament. Storm troopers filled the hall, and communist members had already been arrested. Only the Social Democrats voted no. By July, every party but the Nazis was banned.

The Nazis then brought every group into line, a process called Gleichschaltung. Unions were dissolved. Jewish and opposition civil servants, including teachers, were fired. Books were burned in May. When Hindenburg died in 1934, Hitler became Fuhrer, or leader, and soldiers swore an oath to him personally. A *democracy* had been taken apart largely through legal-looking steps.

words.d: a camp where people are held without trial, often in brutal conditions
the 1933 law that let Hitler's government make laws without the parliament
a system in which citizens choose their leaders in free elections and rights are protected

look.title: A Timeline in Five Steps
look.text: January 30: Hitler becomes chancellor. February 28: an emergency decree suspends free speech and a free press. March 23: the Enabling Act lets the government make laws alone. May 2: trade unions are shut down. July 14: every party but the Nazis is banned.
look.prompt: At which step do you think democracy was lost? Defend your choice with a fact from the reading.

check.q: What did the Enabling Act allow?
choices: All parties to run freely in elections
Hitler's government to make laws without parliament
check.why: The Enabling Act of March 1933 gave lawmaking power to the government alone.

check.q: Which party voted against the Enabling Act, according to the reading?
choices: The Communists, who were in the hall
check.why: Communist members had been arrested; only the Social Democrats voted no.

check.q: What happened right after the Reichstag fire?
choices: An emergency decree suspended free speech, press and assembly
New elections were cancelled forever the same day
check.why: The day after the fire, a decree suspended basic freedoms.

lessons.title: Racial Ideology and Antisemitism
lessons.mainIdea: Nazism rested on a false racial ideology that treated Jews as enemies and stripped them of rights step by step.
reading: At the center of Nazism was *antisemitism*, hatred of Jews. Hitler taught a false *racial ideology*. It claimed that humanity is divided into higher and lower races in a struggle to the death. It cast Jews as a race behind both capitalism and communism. There was no science behind these claims.

Persecution came step by step. In April 1933 the Nazis called a boycott of Jewish shops. The *Nuremberg Laws* of 1935 took away Jews' citizenship and banned marriages between Jews and other Germans. Jewish children were pushed out of schools. Jewish doctors and lawyers lost their right to work.

On November 9 and 10, 1938, Nazi mobs attacked Jewish communities across Germany and Austria. They burned hundreds of synagogues and smashed thousands of shop windows. About 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. The night is called Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass. Many Jews tried to flee, but many countries, including the United States, admitted only limited numbers.

words.d: hostility toward or hatred of Jews
a belief system that ranks human groups as higher or lower races
1935 Nazi laws that stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage with non-Jews
the Nazi attacks on Jews of November 9 and 10, 1938, also called the Night of Broken Glass

look.title: One Street, Five Years
look.text: In 1933 a Jewish tailor on a Berlin street sees a guard outside his shop telling people not to buy from Jews. In 1935 he loses his citizenship. In 1936 his daughter is made to leave her school. In 1938 his windows are smashed and he is taken to a camp for weeks. In 1939 he tries to get a visa to leave.
look.prompt: Why might it have been hard for people to see where these steps were leading? What does this suggest about how persecution grows?

check.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 do?
choices: Took away Jews' citizenship and banned marriages between Jews and other Germans
Ended the boycott of Jewish shops
check.why: The Nuremberg Laws stripped German Jews of citizenship and restricted marriage.

check.q: What was Kristallnacht?
choices: Nazi attacks on Jewish homes, shops and synagogues in November 1938
check.why: Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass, was a wave of attacks on November 9 and 10, 1938.

check.q: According to the reading, what problem did many Jews face when they tried to flee?
choices: Germany required them to stay in the army
They were not allowed to buy train tickets anywhere
Many countries, including the United States, admitted only limited numbers
check.why: The reading says many countries limited how many refugees they admitted.

lessons.title: Genocide Across Europe
lessons.mainIdea: During World War II, Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, along with millions of other victims.
reading: When Germany invaded Poland in 1939 and the Soviet Union in 1941, millions more Jews came under Nazi control. Jews were forced into sealed *ghettos*, like the one in Warsaw, where many starved. Behind the front in the Soviet Union, mobile killing units shot Jews by the hundreds of thousands. At Babi Yar, near Kyiv, nearly 34,000 Jews were shot in two days in September 1941.

In January 1942, Nazi officials met at Wannsee, near Berlin, to coordinate what they called the Final Solution: the murder of all of Europe's Jews. Trains carried families from across Europe to killing centers in occupied Poland, such as Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau. At Auschwitz alone, about 1.1 million people were murdered, most of them Jews.

The *Holocaust* was the murder of about six million Jews, about two out of every three Jews in Europe. The Nazis also murdered Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners of war and others. The word *genocide* was created in 1944 by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin to name crimes like these. Survivors' testimony and the Nazis' own records document what happened.

words.d: the systematic murder of about six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators
sealed city districts where the Nazis forced Jews to live in crowded, starving conditions
acts carried out to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group
people or governments that worked with an occupying enemy

look.title: Victims of Nazi Persecution (rounded estimates)
look.cite: U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, Documenting Numbers of Victims of the Holocaust and Nazi Persecution
look.prompt: Why do historians give ranges for some groups? What does the Museum's careful use of estimates tell you about how history is measured?

check.q: What was decided at the Wannsee meeting in 1942?
choices: How to coordinate the murder of all of Europe's Jews
check.why: At Wannsee officials coordinated the so-called Final Solution.

check.q: About what share of Europe's Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
choices: About two out of every three
check.why: About six million Jews were killed, about two thirds of Europe's Jews.

check.q: Who created the word genocide, and when?
check.why: Lemkin coined the word in 1944 to name crimes like the Holocaust.

lessons.title: Resistance and Rescue
lessons.mainIdea: Even under terror, some people resisted and rescued, showing that choices remained possible.
reading: In April 1943, several hundred young Jewish fighters in the Warsaw Ghetto took up a handful of guns and homemade bombs. They held off German troops for nearly a month. The *Warsaw Ghetto Uprising* was the largest Jewish revolt of the war. The fighters knew they would likely die. They chose to resist on their own terms.

Inside Germany, a few people spoke out. Sophie Scholl and her brother Hans, students in Munich, belonged to the White Rose group. They printed leaflets calling on Germans to resist. In February 1943 they were caught and executed. Others hid Jews in attics and cellars for years, at the risk of their own lives.

Whole communities also acted. In the French village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, Protestant families sheltered thousands of people, many of them Jewish children. In October 1943, people in Denmark helped ferry about 7,000 Jews across the sea to safety in Sweden. Israel's memorial, Yad Vashem, honors non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews as *Righteous Among the Nations*.

words.d: the 1943 armed revolt by Jewish fighters in the Warsaw Ghetto against the Nazis
the honor Yad Vashem gives to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews
actions taken to oppose or undermine those in power

look.title: Many Kinds of Resistance
look.text: A mother in a ghetto teaches her children to read in secret. A student prints leaflets at night. A farmer hides a family under his barn floor. A fighter throws a bomb at a German tank. A fisherman carries refugees across the sea.
look.prompt: Which of these count as resistance? Rank them by the risk each person took, and explain your ranking.

check.q: What was the White Rose?
choices: A French village that hid children
A student group in Munich that printed leaflets against the Nazis
check.why: Sophie and Hans Scholl belonged to the White Rose and were executed in 1943.

check.q: What happened in Denmark in October 1943?
choices: People helped about 7,000 Jews escape by sea to Sweden
Denmark joined the Nazi war on the USSR
check.why: Danes ferried about 7,000 Jews to safety in neutral Sweden.

check.q: Whom does Yad Vashem honor as Righteous Among the Nations?
choices: Soldiers who fought in the Warsaw Ghetto
Non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews
check.why: The title honors non-Jewish rescuers.

sections.title: Other Regimes and a Shared Pattern

lessons.title: Franco's Spain
lessons.mainIdea: General Francisco Franco won Spain's civil war with help from Hitler and Mussolini and ruled as a dictator until 1975.
reading: On April 26, 1937, German and Italian planes bombed the Basque town of Guernica on a market day. Much of the town burned. Pablo Picasso painted a huge canvas, Guernica, that became one of the most famous protests against war. The bombing was part of the *Spanish Civil War*, fought from 1936 to 1939.

The war began when army officers, led by General Francisco Franco, rose against Spain's elected republic. Franco's side, the Nationalists, drew support from many Catholics, landowners and conservatives who feared the left. Hitler and Mussolini sent them troops and planes. The Soviet Union and volunteers from many countries, including Americans in the Abraham Lincoln Brigade, helped the Republicans. Both sides committed killings of civilians.

Franco won in 1939 and ruled as a *dictator* until his death in 1975. Tens of thousands of opponents were executed after the war, and many more were jailed. Franco's regime was built on the army, the Catholic Church and one official party. Historians debate whether it was truly fascist or a conservative military dictatorship. After 1975 Spain made a peaceful transition to democracy.

words.d: the 1936 to 1939 war between Franco's Nationalists and the forces of Spain's elected republic
a ruler with total power who is not limited by elections or courts
Franco's side in the Spanish Civil War

look.title: Reading Picasso's Guernica in Words
look.text: The painting is only black, white and gray. A mother screams, holding a dead child. A horse twists in pain. A bull stands still and stares. A broken sword lies in a fallen soldier's hand. A single light bulb glares over the scene like an eye.
look.prompt: Why might Picasso have painted no planes and no enemy soldiers? What is he asking viewers to look at instead?

check.q: Who helped Franco's Nationalists during the Spanish Civil War?
check.why: Germany and Italy sent troops and planes to Franco; the USSR helped the Republicans.

check.q: What happened at Guernica in 1937?
choices: Spain held its first free election
German and Italian planes bombed the town on a market day
check.why: The bombing of Guernica inspired Picasso's famous painting.

check.q: What do historians debate about Franco's regime?
choices: Whether it was truly fascist or a conservative military dictatorship
Whether Spain became a democracy after 1975
check.why: The reading says historians debate how to label the regime.

lessons.title: Imperial Japan's Militarism
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1930s Japan's military gained control of the government and launched wars of conquest across Asia and the Pacific.
reading: In September 1931 Japanese army officers set off a small explosion on a railway in Manchuria, in northeast China. They blamed Chinese soldiers and used it as an excuse to seize the whole region. Leaders in Tokyo had not ordered the attack, but they accepted it. The military was starting to act on its own.

Japan in the 1930s was not a copy of Nazi Germany. It had no single party and no one dictator. Instead, *militarism*, the belief that the military and its values should lead the nation, took hold. Army officers assassinated politicians who opposed them. Schools taught devotion to the emperor, Hirohito. Censorship silenced critics.

In 1937 Japan launched a full war on China. When Japanese troops took the city of Nanjing that December, they killed large numbers of civilians and prisoners and committed mass rapes. Estimates of the dead range widely and remain disputed, and many historians cite figures in the tens of thousands to around 200,000 or more. In December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, bringing the United States into the war.

words.d: the belief that a country's military and its values should guide the nation
government control over what can be said, printed or shown
the mass killing of Chinese civilians and prisoners by Japanese troops after they captured Nanjing in December 1937

look.title: Comparing Three Regimes
look.text: Italy: one party, one leader, Il Duce. Germany: one party, one leader, the Fuhrer, and a racial ideology at the center. Japan: an emperor treated as sacred, no single ruling party, and army officers who used violence to push the government toward war.
look.prompt: What did all three share? What made Japan different? Use at least two facts from the chapter.

check.q: What is militarism?
choices: A plan to end all armies
The belief that the military and its values should guide the nation
check.why: Militarism puts the military and its values at the center of national life.

check.q: How did Japan's system in the 1930s differ from Nazi Germany's?
choices: It held free elections with many parties
It was run by a communist party
It had no single ruling party and no one dictator
check.why: Japan was driven by military officers and devotion to the emperor, not one party and one dictator.

check.q: What event in 1941 brought the United States into the war with Japan?
check.why: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

lessons.title: Totalitarianism: Where the Extremes Meet
lessons.mainIdea: Hannah Arendt argued in 1951 that Nazi Germany and Stalin's USSR shared a new kind of rule, totalitarianism, built on ideology and terror.
reading: Hannah Arendt was a German Jewish thinker who fled the Nazis in 1933 and later settled in New York. In 1951 she published The Origins of Totalitarianism. She asked how two regimes with opposite stated goals, one on the far right and one on the far left, could come to look so alike in practice.

Arendt described *totalitarianism* as a new form of government. It is not just a harsh dictatorship. It tries to control every part of life, even private thought. It rests on an *ideology* that claims to explain all of history. It uses *terror* against whole groups, not only against real opponents. Nazi Germany and Stalin's USSR, she argued, both fit this model.

Other scholars have added and argued. Some say the model hides real differences: Nazism aimed at racial conquest, while Soviet communism spoke of universal equality. Others say it fits some periods, such as Stalin's rule, better than others. Many agree on a lesson from the century. When one party or leader holds unchecked power in the name of a perfect society, ordinary rights are the first thing lost.

words.d: a form of rule that tries to control every part of public and private life through one party, an ideology and terror
a set of ideas that explains how the world works and what should be done
the use of fear and violence to control a population

look.title: Arendt on Total Domination
look.text: Totalitarian rule differs from older tyranny because it does not stop at controlling public life. It aims to organize people so completely, through ideology and terror, that they lose the ability to act and think for themselves.
look.cite: Hannah Arendt, The Origins of Totalitarianism, 1951 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: How is this different from an ordinary dictatorship? Give one example from Stalin's USSR and one from Nazi Germany that fits Arendt's idea.

check.q: What question did Arendt's 1951 book try to answer?
choices: How regimes with opposite goals on the far left and far right came to look alike
How to build a collective farm
check.why: Arendt compared Nazi Germany and Stalin's USSR as two forms of totalitarianism.

check.q: What makes totalitarianism different from an ordinary dictatorship, in Arendt's view?
choices: It tries to control every part of life, even private thought
It has no ideology at all
check.why: Totalitarian rule reaches into private life through ideology and terror.

check.q: What criticism of the totalitarian model does the reading mention?
choices: It says Nazism and communism had the same goals
It can hide real differences between Nazism and Soviet communism
It was written before World War I
check.why: Some scholars say the model hides differences such as racial conquest versus universal equality.

review.q: Which leader took power after the March on Rome in 1922?
review.why: The king appointed Mussolini prime minister after the March on Rome.

review.q: Which factor helped the Nazis grow in the early 1930s?
choices: Mass unemployment in the Great Depression
A communist government already in power
Germany's victory in World War I
review.why: About six million unemployed and fear of communism boosted the Nazi vote.

review.q: What law let Hitler's government make laws without parliament?
review.why: The Enabling Act of March 1933 ended parliament's lawmaking role.

review.q: About how many Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
review.why: The Holocaust took the lives of about six million Jews.

review.q: Which group besides Jews did the Nazis also murder?
choices: Only members of the Nazi Party
review.why: Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners and others were also killed.

review.q: What did Franco's regime rest on, according to the chapter?

review.q: What feature did Hannah Arendt say Nazi Germany and Stalin's USSR shared?
choices: Total control built on ideology and terror
review.why: Arendt called both totalitarian: one party, an all-explaining ideology and terror.

review.q: What did the burning of books in May 1933 show about the new regime?

review.why: Book burnings were part of bringing all of culture into line with Nazi ideology.
